idiom_name: opaque id + server-owned session record + boundary middleware that resolves and commits it
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: on the first request that needs state, mint a high-entropy identifier (CSPRNG, at least 128 bits) and create an empty record in a store the server owns; send the identifier back in the response carrier with HttpOnly, Secure and a SameSite policy. On every later request, resolve the identifier before application code runs, load the record, and expose it as a session object; after the handler finishes, persist the record and stamp the store-side expiry. Decide explicitly which store backs the record (process memory for one instance, a shared cache or a session table for many), how identifiers are rotated on login, what idle and absolute lifetimes apply, and what happens when the store is unreachable - fail closed for privileged work, fail open only for anonymous traffic. Sweep expired records on a schedule and monitor the store's size, because nothing else will.
code_sketch:
sid  = request.carrier('SESSION')            # cookie or header
rec  = store.load(sid) if sid else None      # server-owned store
if rec is None or expired(rec):
    sid, rec = new_id(), Session.empty()
    store.save(sid, rec, ttl=idle_ttl)
resp.carrier('SESSION', sid, HttpOnly=True, Secure=True, SameSite='Lax')
# later, after the handler:
rec = mutate(rec)
store.save(sid, rec, ttl=idle_ttl)
# sweeper: store.evict(expired_before=now - max_lifetime)
pitfalls: Choosing the store before choosing the deployment: an in-memory record silently becomes 'logged out at the next request' as soon as a second instance exists.
Skipping identifier rotation on login leaves session fixation open - an attacker-planted identifier keeps working after authentication.
Never sweeping expired records turns the store into an unbounded archive of stale conversations (Apache's mod_session_dbd needs an external cron job for exactly this).

Wrong move: assuming the session record is safe under concurrency -> two parallel requests from one client each load, mutate and write back the whole record, and the later write silently discards the earlier one (documented last-writer-wins behaviour of a non-locking coherent session such as ASP.NET Core's) -> instead pick single-writer per conversation, an optimistic version check on the record, or merge-tolerant keys.

Wrong move: caching roles and entitlements in the record at login and consulting that snapshot on every request -> a demoted or suspended user keeps the conversation's privileges until the record expires -> instead store who the principal is and re-derive what they may do from the authoritative source, or version the snapshot with a deliberately short TTL.

Wrong move: leaving store-outage behaviour undefined -> when the shared store fails over, every request either 500s or is silently treated as a fresh anonymous conversation and protected pages render without their record -> instead declare fail-closed (re-authenticate or 503) versus fail-open (continue anonymously) per route group and test both paths.
